texts.preamble: Rajan T vs State Of Kerala on 11 January, 2016 Author: B.Sudheendra Kumar Bench: B.Sudheendra Kumar In The High Court Of Kerala At Ernakulam Present: The Honourable Mr. Justice B.Sudheendra Kumar Monday, The 11Th Day Of January 2016/21St Pousha, 1937 Crl.Rev.Pet.No. 3956 of 2007 ( ) --------------------------------- Crl.A 309/2004 Of The Additional Sessions Court, Fast Track (Adhoc), Mavelikkara Cc 124/2000 Of The Judicial First Class Magistrate Court-I, Chengannur Revision Petitioner/Appellant/Accused: -------------------------------------- Rajan T., Vadakkenarathiyil Padinjattethil, Karazhma West Cherakel P.O., Chennithala, Alappuzha District. By Advs.Sri.P.Vijaya Bhanu Sri.Prasun.S Respondents/Respondents/State & Complainant: ------------------------------------------- 1. State Of Kerala, Represented By Chief Secretary, Thiruvananthapuram Represented By Public Prosecutor High Court Of Kerala, Ernakulam. 2. The Food Inspector, Thattarambalam P.O., Mavelikkara. By Public Prosecutor Sri.R.Githesh This Criminal Revision Petition Having Been Finally Heard Rajan T vs State Of Kerala on 11 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/146336939/ 1 On 11-01-2016, The Court On The Same Day Passed The Following: Scl. B. Sudheendra Kumar, J. ------------------------------------- Crl.R.P. No.3956 of 2007 -------------------------------------- Dated this the 11th day of January, 2016 Order
texts.facts: The accused in S.T.No.124 of 2000 on the files of the Court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class-I, Chengannur, has filed this revision petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Section 2 (ia) (j) and Section 7 (i) r/w Section 16 (1-A) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:- On 21.7.1999 at about 12 noon, PW1, the Food Inspector purchased three packets of sweets, each packet contained 400 gram each, from the shop of the accused. After sampling as per rules, one sample was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis. The Public Analyst, after analysing the sample, filed Ext.P13 report stating that the sample contained synthetic Food Colour in excess of the prescribed limit under Rule 30 of the P.F.A. Rules, 1955 and was therefore adulterated. Thereafter, on the request of the accused, the second sample was sent to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis. Ext.P24 certificate of the Central Food Laboratory would also show that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for Sugar Confectionery laid down under the P.F.A. Rules and was therefore adulterated. 4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW3 were examined and Exts.P1 to P24 were marked for the prosecution. No evidence was adduced on the side of the revision petitioner.
texts.arguments: 5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext. P24 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument. 6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was prescribed as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) Rajan T vs State Of Kerala on 11 January, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/146336939/ 2 (ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act. Therefore, Ext.P24 certificate analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra). It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal. In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
